questions.stem: An operations manager pastes a three-page project status report into Claude and types 'Make this better.' Claude returns a polished version that is actually longer than the original. What she really needed was something the COO could read in under a minute before approving extra budget. Which change to her prompt would MOST directly get the result she needs on the next attempt?

options.text: Say who will read it and why: a one-paragraph summary for the COO that opens with the budget decision needed.
Ask Claude to try again, since a fresh response to the same request may land closer to what she needed.
Begin the prompt by telling Claude it is a world-class business writer before asking it to improve the report.
Switch to the most capable model available so that it can work out on its own what kind of improvement she wants.

questions.explanation: 'Make this better' leaves Claude to guess what 'better' means, so it guessed 'more polished and complete'. Claude follows explicit instructions closely, so the fastest fix is to name the **audience** (the COO), the **purpose** (approve budget) and the **constraint** (one paragraph, decision first). Those three details turn a vague request into a target Claude can hit.

whyWrong.B: Regenerating the same vague request gives Claude no new information about the reader, purpose or length, so a better result would be luck, not design.
whyWrong.C: A role can shape tone, but it does not tell Claude who will read the result, what decision it supports or how short it must be. Those are the missing ingredients.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model still cannot read her mind. 'Better' is ambiguous for every model; the fix is a clearer request, not a bigger model.

questions.mindset: Vague request in, generic output out: name the audience, the goal and the format.

questions.stem: A communications lead uses Claude to draft short announcements for large digital screens in the company's warehouses. Workers walking past only see the first two lines. Her prompt currently says 'Keep it short. No long sentences.' The drafts are short, but the action workers must take and its date often appear at the very end. What is the MOST effective way to improve her instruction?

options.text: Repeat 'KEEP IT SHORT' in capital letters at both the start and the end of the prompt for extra emphasis.
Explain why: only the first two lines show on the warehouse screens, so the action and its date must always come first.
Set a strict word limit for each announcement and ask Claude to count the words before it replies.
Ask Claude for five versions of every announcement so she can pick the one with the best opening lines.

questions.explanation: Claude's prompting guidance recommends explaining **why** an instruction matters, not just stating the rule. Once Claude knows readers only see the first two lines of a screen, it can work out the right behavior on its own: lead with the action and the date. A bare rule like 'keep it short' gets followed literally and misses the real goal.

whyWrong.A: The drafts are already short. Shouting the same rule louder does not tell Claude that the order of information matters, which is the real problem.
whyWrong.C: A word limit controls length, which is already fine. It says nothing about putting the action and date first, so key details can still land at the end.
whyWrong.D: Generating many options shifts the work back to her for every announcement and still leaves Claude unaware of why the opening lines matter.

questions.mindset: Give the reason behind a rule and Claude can apply it sensibly to cases you did not spell out.

questions.stem: An e-commerce marketing coordinator uses Claude to write product descriptions for 200 items, from scented candles to phone chargers. Her prompt contains a paragraph describing the brand voice, but the results vary widely in structure and tone. Which change is MOST likely to make the descriptions consistent?

options.text: Add one approved candle description and tell Claude to follow it exactly for every product in the catalog.
Expand the brand-voice paragraph with more adjectives, such as warm, playful, confident and premium.
Add three to five approved descriptions for different product types, clearly marked as examples of the tone and structure.
Ask Claude to finish each description by confirming that it matched the brand voice before moving on.

questions.explanation: Examples are among the most reliable ways to steer Claude's format, tone and structure. Anthropic's guidance suggests **3-5 examples** that are **relevant** (close to the real task), **diverse** (covering different cases, so Claude does not copy one item's quirks) and **clearly marked** as examples. A range of approved descriptions across product types shows the shared pattern far better than adjectives can.

whyWrong.A: A single example tends to be copied too closely. Candle-specific wording such as scent notes would leak into charger descriptions. Varied examples show the pattern without one item's quirks.
whyWrong.B: More abstract adjectives leave the same room for interpretation. Concrete examples show Claude the target far more reliably than further description of it.
whyWrong.D: A self-confirmation adds text but no new information. Claude will usually say yes, and the inconsistency comes from an unclear target, not a lack of checking.

questions.mindset: Show, don't just tell: several varied examples beat a longer description of the style.

questions.stem: A procurement analyst pastes three supplier contracts (about 40 pages each) into a single message. Her message opens with the question 'Which contract has the most favorable termination terms, and what notice period does each require?', followed by the three contracts pasted one after another with no labels. Claude sometimes attributes a clause to the wrong supplier. With minimal extra effort, which revision is MOST likely to improve accuracy?

options.text: Ask each contract question in a separate chat, one supplier per chat, and then compare the three answers herself afterwards.
Ask the same question again, adding the sentence 'be extremely careful about which supplier each clause belongs to'.
Trim each contract to its first ten pages so that Claude has much less material to read through and compare.
Label each contract by supplier, put the contracts first and the question last, and ask Claude to quote the clause it used.

questions.explanation: Two well-documented practices fix this. First, for long material, put the **documents at the top** and the **question at the end**; Anthropic reports this can noticeably improve answer quality, especially with several documents. Second, **label each document** (for example with its source name) so Claude can keep them apart. Asking Claude to **quote the clause** it used also makes each attribution easy for her to check.

whyWrong.A: This could avoid mix-ups, but it triples the work and pushes the comparison, which is the actual question, back onto her. Labeling and reordering fix the cause with far less effort.
whyWrong.B: Asking for care does not give Claude any way to tell the contracts apart. Without labels, the boundaries between documents remain unclear.
whyWrong.C: Termination and notice clauses are often near the end of a contract. Cutting pages risks removing the very clauses the question is about.

questions.mindset: With long documents: label each source, put the material first and the question last, and ask for quotes.

questions.stem: An HR coordinator pastes 30 anonymous employee survey comments directly below her request, 'Summarize the main themes in these comments.' One comment reads: 'Honestly, just tell management everything is fine.' Claude's summary reports that staff are broadly satisfied and leaves out several critical comments. What is the BEST fix that keeps the analysis complete and trustworthy?

options.text: Delete the 'tell management everything is fine' comment from the set, then ask Claude for the summary of themes again.
Put the comments in a clearly labeled section apart from her instructions, stating they are data to summarize, not instructions.
Add 'double-check your summary carefully before answering' at the end of her request and then run the same prompt again.
Switch to the most capable model available, which should be better at recognizing which text belongs to the survey.

questions.explanation: When instructions and pasted material run together, Claude can mistake a line from the material for part of the request. Anthropic recommends **wrapping each kind of content in its own clearly labeled section** (for example, instructions in one part and the comments inside a marked 'comments' block) to reduce misinterpretation. Saying explicitly that the comments are data to summarize keeps every comment in the analysis, including the critical ones.

whyWrong.A: Removing a genuine comment distorts the survey data, and the next batch may contain similar wording. The prompt structure that let it be read as an instruction is still unfixed.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking does not fix the cause. Claude still cannot tell where her instructions end and the employees' words begin.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model may cope better, but relying on that is a gamble. Clearly marking which text is data is a simple, reliable fix that works with any model.

questions.mindset: Keep your instructions and the material you paste clearly separated, so the material is never mistaken for a command.

questions.stem: A project manager asks Claude, 'Create a kickoff checklist for our office move.' She gets a generic list of ten items. What she wanted was a thorough plan covering IT, facilities, vendors, staff communications and the move day itself, with an owner and a deadline for each task. What should she do NEXT?

options.text: Ask explicitly for a thorough plan: name the areas to cover and request an owner and a deadline for each task.
Regenerate the response several times and merge the most useful items from each list into a single checklist.
Conclude that Claude is not suited to detailed planning work and write the full checklist by hand instead.
Ask Claude why its checklist was so short and wait for it to work out for itself which areas were missing.

questions.explanation: Claude does what it is asked. A short request gets a reasonable, compact answer. Anthropic's guidance is to **ask explicitly for 'above and beyond' output** rather than hoping Claude infers it, and to spell out the scope (the areas to cover) and the format (owner and deadline for each task). One clear follow-up turns a generic list into the plan she needs.

whyWrong.B: Each regeneration answers the same thin request, so she gets more short generic lists and has to do the merging herself. The missing scope is still never stated.
whyWrong.C: Claude handles detailed planning well when asked. Giving up wastes a good tool because of a fixable prompt problem.
whyWrong.D: Claude cannot know which areas she had in mind. Asking it to guess why it missed them is slower than simply stating what she wants.

questions.mindset: If you want comprehensive output, say so and define the scope; Claude will not assume it.

questions.stem: An HR generalist asks Claude to draft answers to frequently asked questions about her company's parental-leave policy for the new-hire portal. The draft reads well, but it includes week counts and eligibility rules that do not match the company's actual policy. Which change to her prompt is MOST effective?

options.text: Ask Claude to use its knowledge of typical parental-leave policies at similar companies so that the answers sound realistic.
Add the sentence 'Make sure every fact in these answers is accurate' at the end of the existing prompt.
Attach the current policy, tell Claude to answer only from it, and have it flag any question the policy doesn't cover.
Turn on web search so Claude can find the company's parental-leave policy online and base the answers on that.

questions.explanation: Claude does not know your organization's internal facts, so when asked about them it may produce plausible-sounding but wrong details. The fix is to **provide the source material** and **restrict Claude to it**, while giving it **permission to say when something is not covered**. Anthropic recommends both techniques for reducing invented content. She should still check the final answers before they go live.

whyWrong.A: This invites exactly the problem she has: plausible general figures that are not her company's rules. Realistic is not the same as correct.
whyWrong.B: Claude cannot be accurate about an internal policy it has never seen. Without the source document, the instruction has nothing to check against.
whyWrong.D: Internal HR policies are usually not public, and anything found online may be outdated or about a different company. The authoritative source is the document she already has.

questions.mindset: For internal facts, supply the source and tell Claude to answer only from it.

questions.stem: A sales director types into Claude: 'Write a quarterly update for the board.' The first draft is generic and uses placeholder numbers. Which TWO changes to her approach would MOST improve the next draft? Choose TWO.

options.text: An opening line telling Claude that it is the most talented executive writer in the world.
Adding who the board members are and what decision or feedback the update needs to get from them at this meeting.
A closing line asking Claude to be accurate, professional and appropriate for a board audience.
Switching to the most capable model available, since a stronger model needs fewer details to produce a strategic, board-ready draft.
Supplying the real quarter figures to include, plus the structure and length wanted, such as four sections within two pages.

questions.explanation: A strong business prompt covers **audience and purpose** (who reads it and what it must achieve) and supplies the **source material and format** (the real figures, sections and length). Claude cannot invent your actual quarter results, and without a stated purpose it cannot decide what to emphasize. These two additions remove most of the guesswork.

whyWrong.A: Flattering the model adds no information about the board, the goal or the figures, which are what the generic draft is missing.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot be accurate about numbers it was never given, and 'professional' is too vague to change much. The draft needs real inputs, not adjectives.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model still cannot know the board's priorities or the real figures. Any model will produce a generic draft from a generic request.

questions.mindset: Give Claude the facts it cannot know and the purpose it cannot guess.

questions.stem: A finance analyst pastes a long spreadsheet formula that is slow and hard to maintain, and asks Claude, 'Can you suggest some ways this formula could be improved?' Claude replies with a list of general ideas. She actually wanted a rewritten formula she could paste straight back into the sheet. What is the BEST way to phrase her follow-up?

options.text: Accept the list of ideas and apply them herself one at a time, since Claude is better at advice than at rewriting.
Ask Claude to rank its suggestions from most to least useful so she knows which idea to try first.
Open a new chat and ask exactly the same question again, hoping that this time the reply includes a rewrite.
Ask directly for the rewrite: explain what each referenced column holds and request only the new formula with a short note.

questions.explanation: Claude answers the request it was given. Phrased as a question about ways the formula could be improved, the natural reply is a list of ideas. **Being clear and direct** means asking for exactly the output she wants, the rewritten formula, and adding the context it needs, such as what each referenced column holds, so the result can go straight into the sheet.

whyWrong.A: Claude can rewrite the formula itself. The list came from how the request was worded, not from a limit of the tool, so she takes on avoidable work.
whyWrong.B: Ranking still produces advice, not the rewritten formula she needs. It refines the wrong output.
whyWrong.C: The same wording asks for suggestions again, so a rewrite would be luck. Starting over also loses the formula context already shared.

questions.mindset: Ask for the action you want, not for suggestions about it.

questions.stem: A middle-school English teacher uses Claude to draft written feedback on her 13- and 14-year-old students' persuasive essays. The feedback is accurate but full of advanced terms, and several students found it discouraging. Which TWO prompt changes would MOST improve the feedback? Choose TWO.

options.text: Say that 13- and 14-year-olds will read it, so use words they know, open with a real strength and give at most two next steps.
Tell Claude it is a renowned university literature professor so that its feedback carries more authority.
Add 'BE NICE' in capital letters at the very top of the prompt so that the tone instruction cannot be missed.
Include the class rubric for persuasive essays and say which of its criteria the feedback should focus on for this assignment.
Ask Claude to rate how age-appropriate its feedback is on a scale of 1 to 10 after each essay it reviews.

questions.explanation: The problem has two causes: Claude was not told **who the reader is**, and it had no **criteria** to anchor its comments. Naming the audience (students aged 13-14), the tone and the structure (strength first, at most two next steps) fixes the language. Supplying the **rubric** keeps the feedback tied to what the teacher actually grades. Both are specific, checkable instructions rather than vague adjectives.

whyWrong.B: This role points in the wrong direction: it invites more academic language for an audience that needs simpler words.
whyWrong.C: Shouting a vague word gives no guidance on vocabulary, structure or how much criticism to include. Specific audience details do that.
whyWrong.E: A self-rating is not evidence of quality and does not change how the feedback is written in the first place.

questions.mindset: Describe the real reader and give the real criteria; vague tone words and flattering roles don't do that.

questions.stem: A marketing analyst asks Claude to estimate the market size for a new product in five regions, attaching an industry report that only has data for two of them. Claude returns a confident total for all five regions, with nothing showing that three were estimated. She plans to reuse this prompt every month for leadership updates. Which prompt change is MOST effective?

options.text: Ask Claude to add a confidence score after each figure, and only use the months where every score comes back high.
Drop the three regions without data from the request permanently, so that Claude only reports the two regions with data.
Restrict Claude to the attached report, have it label any unsupported figure as an assumption, and say where data is lacking.
Add the instruction 'Use your expert knowledge to fill in missing regions with realistic numbers' so the total stays complete.

questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends **giving Claude explicit permission to say it does not know** and **restricting it to the provided material**. Both reduce invented content. Here the business still needs all five regions, so the right prompt keeps the full request but makes Claude **separate sourced figures from assumptions** and flag gaps. Leadership then sees which numbers are solid and which are estimates.

whyWrong.A: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable signal of accuracy. Claude was already confident about figures it had no data for.
whyWrong.B: Leadership still needs a view of all five regions. This hides the gap instead of making it visible and changes the business question to fit the data.
whyWrong.D: This openly asks for unsupported figures dressed up as real ones, which is exactly the risk in a leadership update.

questions.mindset: Let Claude say 'the data doesn't cover this' and make it label assumptions, rather than letting it fill gaps silently.

questions.stem: A team lead has written a reusable Claude prompt template for weekly client status emails. Before sharing it with 12 account managers, she wants a quick way to check that the template is clear enough to give good results. Which check is MOST useful?

options.text: Add every rule the team has ever discussed about client emails so that nothing at all can be left out.
Ask a colleague unfamiliar with these accounts to try following it, then fix whatever confused them or raised questions.
Ask Claude to score the template out of 10 and share it with the team if the score comes back at 8 or higher.
Share it with the account managers right away and collect their complaints at the end of the first month.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's 'golden rule' for prompting: **show the prompt to a colleague who has little context on the task**. If they would be confused, Claude probably will be too. It is a fast, low-cost clarity check before a template spreads to a whole team, and trying it on a few real weeks' inputs is a natural next step.

whyWrong.A: Piling on rules makes the template longer and harder to follow, and it doesn't tell her whether the existing wording is clear.
whyWrong.C: A self-assigned score isn't a reliable measure of clarity. It gives false confidence without testing the template on anyone.
whyWrong.D: This tests the template on real client emails for a month. A quick check before release catches problems much more cheaply.

questions.mindset: If a new colleague couldn't follow your prompt, Claude can't either.

questions.stem: An IT support lead asks Claude to write a step-by-step guide that office staff can follow when their laptops cannot connect to the shared printer. The first draft assumes the wrong operating system and includes steps that need administrator rights, which staff do not have. Which change to the prompt is MOST effective?

options.text: Ask for a guide that covers every operating system and permission level so that it works for anyone who reads it.
State the real setup: the operating system, the printer model, no admin rights for staff, and no steps that need IT tools.
Add the instruction 'be technically precise and accurate' to the current request and ask for the guide again.
Tell Claude to act as a senior IT engineer with many years of experience fixing office printer problems.

questions.explanation: For technical tasks, missing **environment details and constraints** are a common cause of unusable output. Claude cannot see your office setup, so it fills gaps with common defaults. Stating the operating system, printer model, staff permissions and the 'no IT tools' limit lets Claude write steps the actual audience can carry out.

whyWrong.A: A guide for every possible setup is long and confusing for staff, and most of it would not apply to them. Stating their real setup gives a shorter, usable guide.
whyWrong.C: The draft was precise, just for the wrong environment. Without the actual setup details, Claude has to guess again.
whyWrong.D: Expertise doesn't reveal which operating system the office uses or that staff lack admin rights. A senior-engineer framing may even add more admin-level steps.

questions.mindset: In technical prompts, state the environment and the constraints; Claude will otherwise assume common defaults.

questions.stem: A customer support team lead is writing a prompt so Claude can help agents draft replies to customers complaining about delayed orders. Early drafts are polite but generic, sometimes promise refunds the company does not offer for delays, and sound nothing like the brand. Which TWO changes address the root causes MOST directly? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add 'NEVER promise anything you shouldn't' in capital letters near the top so the warning is impossible to miss.
Ask Claude to write ten versions of each reply so the agent can choose the one that sounds most on-brand.
Include the current compensation policy for delayed orders and state that replies may offer only the remedies it lists.
Move to the most capable model, since generic and off-brand replies usually point to a model that isn't capable enough.
Add several approved past replies covering different complaint situations, clearly marked as examples of the brand's voice.

questions.explanation: Each symptom has a specific cause. Invented refunds come from **missing source material**: Claude doesn't know the real policy, so supply it and limit offers to it. Generic, off-brand tone comes from **no concrete target**: a few varied, approved replies marked as examples show the voice better than any description. Agents should still review each reply before sending.

whyWrong.A: Claude can't know what it 'shouldn't' promise without the policy. A vague prohibition doesn't supply the missing facts.
whyWrong.B: This multiplies agent workload on every ticket and still leaves both root causes, the missing policy and the missing voice examples, unfixed.
whyWrong.D: The drafts are generic because Claude lacks the policy and examples of the brand voice. A larger model still has neither.

questions.mindset: Match each fix to its cause: missing facts need source material; missing voice needs examples.

questions.stem: An executive assistant asks Claude to draft a warm thank-you email to a major donor. Her prompt is laid out with headings and bullet lists, and it ends with 'Don't use bullet points.' The drafts keep coming back with bullet lists and section headings. Which TWO changes are MOST likely to fix this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Describe the form she does want: three or four short, warm paragraphs of flowing prose, written like a personal letter.
Repeat 'NO BULLETS' several times throughout the prompt so that the instruction outweighs everything else in it.
Ask Claude to check each draft before sending it back and to confirm that it contains no bullet points or headings.
Switch to a faster, lighter model, since smaller models tend to write simpler replies with less formatting.
Paste in one of her own hand-written donor thank-yous, clearly marked as an example of the exact tone and form to match.

questions.explanation: A ban on bullets leaves the target undefined: Claude is told what to avoid but not what to produce. Two verified fixes apply. First, **be clear and direct about the format wanted**: describe the flowing-prose letter in positive terms (three or four short, warm paragraphs). Second, **constrain with an example**: Anthropic's guidance says examples are more effective than abstract instructions for conveying format and tone, and one of her own approved notes is the exact target.

whyWrong.B: Repeating a negative rule still tells Claude only what to avoid, not what to produce. Emphasis adds no information about the desired form.
whyWrong.C: A self-check happens after the draft is written, so it cannot change how it is written, and a confirmation is not a reliable control.
whyWrong.D: Formatting is driven by instructions and examples, not model size. The same prompt on a lighter model will produce similar bullet-heavy drafts.

questions.mindset: Specify the format you want in positive terms, and anchor tone and form with a real example.
